opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot robotics can learn from autonomous driving, both from what went right and from what took much longer than people expected.

The first lesson is about data. Autonomous driving showed that the long tail is everything. Getting a car to drive well 95% of the time was relatively fast. The last few percent, the weird construction zones, the unusual pedestrian behavior, the rare weather, took years and billions of dollars. Robotics is going to face the same thing, probably even more severely, because a household or a factory is far more diverse than a road. Roads at least have lane markings and traffic rules. A kitchen has none of that. So the question of how you systematically collect, curate, and learn from long-tail data is central, and the driving industry has built a lot of infrastructure and intuition around it: fleet data collection, triggering on interesting events, simulation for rare scenarios, closed-loop evaluation.

The second lesson is the shift from modular pipelines to end-to-end learning. For a long time driving stacks were hand-engineered: perception, prediction, planning, control, each tuned separately. Over the last few years the field moved toward more end-to-end models, and that shift happened once there was enough data and compute. Robotics is going through a similar transition right now with vision-language-action models. The driving experience suggests the end-to-end approach wins in the long run, but you still need a lot of engineering discipline around it: safety layers, evaluation, interpretability tools, ways to debug when the model does something wrong.

Third is evaluation. One of the hardest problems in driving was simply knowing whether a new model is better than the old one. You can't just look at a benchmark. You need large-scale simulation, replay of real logs, and carefully designed metrics. Robotics today is quite weak here. A lot of results are a few dozen real-world trials in a lab. If we want to scale, we need evaluation that's as rigorous as what the driving companies eventually built.

And finally there's a lesson about timelines and business models. Driving went through a hype cycle where people promised full autonomy in a couple of years, then a long disillusionment, and only now is it really working commercially in some cities. I think robotics should be honest about that. The path probably isn't jumping straight to a general-purpose humanoid in every home. It's finding constrained settings where the robot can be useful today, deploying there, gathering data, and expanding the operational domain step by step, much like robotaxis expanded city by city.

So I'd say: take the data flywheel, the evaluation rigor, and the patience from driving, while recognizing that manipulation and open-world interaction make robotics an even harder version of the same problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest lesson is that autonomous driving went through the whole cycle first, and robotics gets to watch the replay.

The first thing is about the data engine. Ten years ago, driving was a modular pipeline. You had perception, prediction, planning, and control as separate boxes with hand-written interfaces between them. Every company believed that was the only responsible way to build a safety-critical system. Then, over time, the industry moved toward end-to-end learning, because the modular approach hit a ceiling. The long tail of edge cases was too long to cover with rules. What made end-to-end possible was not just the model. It was the infrastructure around it. A fleet of cars, a way to find the rare scenarios, a way to label or auto-label them, a closed loop where you deploy, collect, retrain, and deploy again. Robotics today is roughly where driving was before that transition. Everyone agrees the model should be learned. But very few teams have the data flywheel. So the lesson is, do not fall in love with the model architecture. Build the loop.

The second lesson is about simulation. Driving taught us that simulation is useful but it will lie to you if you let it. The sim-to-real gap in driving was mostly about sensors and about the behavior of other agents. In robotics it is worse, because contact physics is hard to simulate. Grasping a deformable object, friction, cable dynamics. So you should use simulation the way driving eventually used it, as a tool to test and to stress rare situations, not as the primary source of training data for the final policy. Real data has to dominate.

The third lesson, which I think people underestimate, is the operational side. Driving companies learned that the product is not the model. The product is the whole system, including the safety case, the remote assistance, the way you handle failure gracefully. A robot in a warehouse or a home will fail. The question is whether it fails safely and whether you have a way to recover without a human running over every time. Driving spent years on that and robotics can borrow most of it directly.

And one thing I would say robotics should not copy. Driving had the luxury of one task. Go from A to B without hitting anything. Robotics has thousands of tasks. So the data problem is not just scale, it is diversity. You cannot drive a million miles of the same thing. You need many embodiments, many environments, many skills. That is actually where I think the two fields will diverge, and where the foundation-model approach from language becomes more relevant than the driving playbook.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest lesson is that a compelling demo and a reliable product are very different things. In autonomous driving, you can handle many everyday situations and still struggle with the rare cases. Robotics faces that same challenge: picking up an object once is very different from doing it reliably across different objects, lighting conditions, and environments.

So robotics can learn a lot from the development loop: collect data, identify failures, improve the system, and test whether those failures are actually resolved. Simulation can help, but you still need feedback from the real world.

The other lesson is to define the operating conditions carefully. Instead of trying to build a robot that can do everything immediately, start with a useful task in an environment you can understand and measure. Make it dependable, then expand.

But the analogy has limits. Robots physically change their environment. When you grasp something, your action changes what happens next, and mistakes can be difficult to undo. So I would borrow the discipline of autonomous driving, without assuming its entire technical approach transfers directly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest lesson is that building an impressive demo and building a reliable system are very different things. Autonomous driving forces you to confront that gap: how do you collect useful data, measure progress, and understand the situations where your system fails?

Robotics needs that same discipline. When a robot fails at a task, you want that failure to feed into a repeatable process—collect the data, improve the model, and test whether you actually fixed the problem without creating another one.

But we also have to be careful about the analogy. Driving has a relatively consistent interface: steering, acceleration, braking. Robots can have very different bodies, and manipulating an object changes the environment through contact. So I’d borrow the data and evaluation infrastructure from autonomous driving, while being careful about assuming the same methods will transfer directly.
